statement: The Hessian matrix of a scalar-valued function f (a scalar field) is the square matrix of its second-order partial derivatives; it describes the local curvature of a function of many variables. It is denoted H or ∇²f. [wikipedia:Hessian_matrix]

symbols.meaning: point / vector of n variables at which the function is evaluated
Hessian matrix of f at x, the square matrix of second-order partial derivatives

properties.property: H governs the quadratic term of the second-order Taylor expansion of f: f(x+Δx) ≈ f(x) + ∇f(x)^T Δx + (1/2) Δx^T H(x) Δx
properties.why: the Hessian is the coefficient matrix of the second-order term in the local expansion of f

properties.property: Computing and storing the full Hessian costs Θ(n²) memory, which is infeasible for high-dimensional functions (e.g. neural-net or CRF loss functions); truncated-Newton and quasi-Newton algorithms (e.g. BFGS) use approximations to H instead
properties.why: the matrix has n² entries, one per pair of variables

properties.property: H also appears in the local expansion of the gradient itself: ∇f(x+Δx) = ∇f(x) + H(x)Δx + O(‖Δx‖²), so a Hessian-vector product H(x)v can be approximated as (1/r)[∇f(x+rv) − ∇f(x)] + O(r) without forming H explicitly
properties.why: lets optimization algorithms that only need H acting as a linear operator avoid materializing the full matrix

properties.property: For a vector-valued function f: R^n → R^m, the second partial derivatives form a third-order tensor equal to a stack of m ordinary Hessians, H(f) = (H(f_1), H(f_2), …, H(f_m)), which degenerates to the usual Hessian when m = 1
properties.why: each component function f_i of a vector field has its own scalar Hessian

properties.property: Under an equality constraint g(x) = c, the relevant object is the bordered Hessian — the Hessian of the Lagrangian Λ(x,λ) = f(x) + λ[g(x) − c] — with a top-left m×m zero block and the constraint gradients ∂g/∂x as borders, used for the second-derivative test in constrained optimization
properties.why: the unconstrained Hessian's definiteness test no longer applies once the domain is restricted to the constraint surface

assumptions.assumption: f is scalar-valued and possesses well-defined second-order partial derivatives at x
assumptions.breaks_when: f is vector-valued (m>1), in which case the second-derivative object is a third-order tensor (an array of m Hessians) rather than a single matrix

failure_modes.mode: Full Hessian is computationally infeasible to form or store
failure_modes.signature: n (number of parameters) is large, e.g. neural-network loss functions, requiring Θ(n²) memory
failure_modes.cause: the Hessian has n² entries; quasi-Newton/truncated-Newton methods (e.g. BFGS) substitute approximations rather than computing H exactly

failure_modes.mode: Finite-difference approximation of a Hessian-vector product becomes numerically unstable
failure_modes.signature: result is inaccurate whether the step scalar r is made very small or left larger
failure_modes.cause: H(x)v ≈ (1/r)[∇f(x+rv) − ∇f(x)] trades truncation error O(r) against floating-point cancellation error as r → 0, so no single r is safe
